Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Do not use dashes, semicolons, colons or parentheses.

text:
On April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted Apollo 13 from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. It carried three men toward the third landing on the Moon. James Lovell was the commander, a veteran of three earlier flights who was making his second trip around the Moon. Fred Haise was the lunar module pilot, new to space. The command module pilot was John Swigert, who had joined the crew only days before. The original pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles, and doctors grounded him. Swigert trained hard in the last few days and the crew settled into a routine journey.

The astronauts named their command module Odyssey and their lunar module Aquarius. The two craft were joined nose to nose, with a service module behind Odyssey holding the engine, the fuel cells and the tanks of oxygen and hydrogen. Those supplies fed the fuel cells, which made the ship's electricity and drinking water. For two days almost nothing went wrong. The crew even gave a television broadcast from space, touring the ship for an audience on Earth that barely tuned in.

The trouble began long before launch. One of the two oxygen tanks in the service module had been dropped slightly during handling at the factory. Later, during a ground test, a heater inside it was exposed to a higher voltage than it was built for, and its protective switches fused shut. The heater cooked the wire insulation, leaving bare copper inside a tank of liquid oxygen. Nobody knew. The tank passed its checks and flew.

On the evening of April 13, about fifty five hours into the flight and more than three hundred thousand kilometers from home, Mission Control asked the crew to stir the oxygen tanks, a routine step to keep the contents evenly mixed. Swigert flipped the switch. A spark jumped across the damaged wires and the oxygen caught fire. Pressure surged inside the tank until it burst, and the blast tore off a panel on the side of the service module.

The crew heard a bang and felt the ship shudder. Swigert reported, "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here." Lovell repeated it a moment later. On the ground, flight controllers watched their screens fill with strange readings. Pressure in one oxygen tank was falling, and then the second tank began to leak as well. Power on the main electrical lines sagged. Within minutes Lovell looked out of a window and saw a stream of gas venting into space. He told Houston plainly that the ship was losing its oxygen.

The fuel cells could not run without oxygen. Odyssey was dying, and with it went any hope of landing on the Moon. Flight director Gene Kranz gathered his team and set a new goal. The mission was now about getting three men home alive.

Aquarius became the lifeboat. The lunar module was built to carry two men for two days on the Moon, and now it had to sustain three men for four days. Lovell and Haise climbed into it, and Swigert followed after shutting Odyssey down to save its batteries for the last hours of the trip. Those batteries would be needed for the fall through the atmosphere. Everything else had to be powered off or saved.

The next question was the route. Apollo 13 had been aimed on a path that would have missed the Earth if nothing changed, so engineers considered turning around at once. That would have required using the damaged service module engine, which no one trusted. Instead they chose to swing around the far side of the Moon, letting its gravity bend the path back toward Earth. About two hours after passing the Moon, the crew fired the lunar module's descent engine to speed up the return. The ship reached a distance of nearly four hundred thousand kilometers from Earth, farther than any humans have travelled before or since.

Life aboard was hard. With almost no power the cabin grew cold, and the temperature fell to just above freezing. Moisture beaded on the walls. The crew slept little and wore the warmest clothes they had. Water was rationed to a few spoonfuls a day, and Haise came down with a fever. The astronauts were thirsty, exhausted and cold for most of the flight home.

A more urgent threat was the air itself. Carbon dioxide from their breathing was building up faster than the lunar module's filters could remove it. Spare filters existed in the command module, but they were square and the receptacles in the lunar module were round. Engineers on the ground gathered the same items the crew had on board, including plastic bags, cardboard, hoses and duct tape, and worked out a way to join one to the other. They read the instructions to the astronauts step by step. The crew built the device and the carbon dioxide level dropped. The homemade adapter is one of the best known pieces of improvisation in the history of flight.

Navigation was another puzzle. Without the usual guidance system the crew used the Sun and the shape of the Earth's shadow to hold the ship on course. When the Earth drifted away from its aiming point, they had to burn the engine by hand for a correction. Meanwhile Mattingly, who had been left behind, spent long hours in a simulator with engineers working out how to restart the command module from a cold, nearly powerless state. The procedure had never been attempted before. Mission Control sent it up to the crew in sequence, and the astronauts copied it down in the cold.

On April 17 the crew prepared for the last stage. First they cut away the service module. As it drifted off, they saw for the first time how bad the damage was. A whole side panel was gone and the equipment inside was scarred and twisted. Lovell reported it to Houston and engineers studied the photographs. Then the crew moved back into Odyssey, powered it up, and released Aquarius, which had served them so well. The lunar module fell behind and burned up later in the atmosphere.

Reentry was the final test. As Odyssey plunged into the air, a hot sheath of plasma blocked radio contact. Usually that silence lasts about three minutes. This time it stretched longer, because the angle of descent was a little shallower than normal. Flight controllers stared at the silent speakers. Eventually a call came through. Swigert's voice returned to the radio, and the control room erupted.

Three parachutes bloomed. Odyssey settled into the South Pacific near Samoa, within sight of the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima. The flight had lasted nearly six days. The astronauts came aboard tired, thinner and unshaven but in good health. They had not walked on the Moon, but Apollo 13 became known as a successful failure, a mission that tested human ingenuity far more than a normal landing ever could.

The investigation that followed pinned the cause on the damaged tank and its heater. NASA redesigned the oxygen tanks, removed the dangerous wiring and added a spare supply of power. The lunar program went on to fly Apollo 14 and later missions, and the lessons of Apollo 13 reshaped how spacecraft were built and how teams prepared for the unexpected. The story endures because it shows people, in a place with no easy exits, working a problem together until they found a way home.
